subtopic_detail: Nocturnal hand paraesthesiae relieved by shaking with normal strength on examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 52 year old woman who wakes most nights with pins and needles in her right hand and has to hang it over the side of the bed and shake it for relief.

The tingling affects the thumb, index and middle fingers and she has begun dropping her coffee cup in the mornings. She works as a hairdresser. Sensation to light touch is reduced over the palmar aspect of the radial three digits with normal sensation over the thenar eminence itself. Abductor pollicis brevis power is full and there is no visible wasting. Neck movements are full and painless and do not reproduce the symptoms, and reflexes in both arms are normal and symmetrical. Her thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin measured last month were normal.

data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over palmar thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, abductor pollicis brevis power 5 out of 5, no thenar wasting, full painless neck range, biceps and triceps reflexes normal and symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.4 percent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Provide a neutral position wrist splint to be worn overnight and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Nocturnal paraesthesiae in a median distribution relieved by shaking, with sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the nerve before the tunnel, is characteristic median nerve compression at the wrist without motor loss. A neutral position night splint is effective first line treatment for mild to moderate disease and avoids both injection and surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies before offering any treatment for her hand symptoms at this stage
options.rationale: Electrophysiology confirms the diagnosis and grades severity and is required before surgery or when the picture is atypical, but it is not needed to start conservative treatment in a classic presentation. Studies are also normal in a proportion of symptomatic patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical decompression of the nerve to prevent irreversible loss of thenar muscle bulk
options.rationale: Urgent decompression is driven by thenar wasting, persistent sensory loss or severe changes on nerve conduction studies, and none are present here since power is full and there is no wasting. Surgery remains available if conservative treatment fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange cervical spine imaging to investigate a C6 radiculopathy as the cause of her arm symptoms
options.rationale: A cervical root lesion typically produces neck pain, symptoms provoked by neck movement, and altered reflexes, and its sensory territory extends above the wrist. Painless full neck movement with normal symmetrical reflexes argues against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral pregabalin titrated over two weeks to control the neuropathic symptoms in the hand
options.rationale: Neuromodulator drugs treat neuropathic pain but do not relieve a mechanical compression and carry sedation, dizziness and weight gain. Evidence in this condition is poor compared with splinting or decompression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and presents with nocturnal paraesthesiae in the median distribution that patients relieve by shaking or hanging the hand. A characteristic examination finding is preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and is therefore spared, which helps distinguish it from a more proximal median lesion or a C6 radiculopathy. Provocative tests such as Tinel and Phalen have modest sensitivity and specificity and do not exclude the diagnosis when negative. Associated conditions worth screening for include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly. Management for mild to moderate disease begins with a neutral position night splint, with corticosteroid injection as a second option, while surgical decompression is indicated for thenar wasting, persistent sensory loss, severe electrophysiological changes or failed conservative treatment.
key_points: Nocturnal symptoms relieved by shaking the hand is the classic history
Sparing of the thenar eminence reflects the palmar cutaneous branch leaving proximally
Nerve conduction studies grade severity and precede surgery, not conservative treatment
Screen for hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly
Thenar wasting or persistent sensory loss moves management to decompression
explanation.pearls: Fit the splint in the neutral position rather than in extension, because the pressure within the carpal tunnel is lowest with the wrist straight and rises with both flexion and extension, so a wrist support designed for sporting use can worsen the very symptoms it is meant to relieve.

subtopic_detail: Deranged liver enzymes with a new movement disorder in a young adult
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 22 year old university student referred with abnormal liver enzymes found when he was investigated for fatigue. His mother mentions separately that his handwriting has deteriorated over the past year and that his speech has become slurred at times.

He drinks around four standard drinks a week, takes no regular medication and no supplements, and has never injected drugs. He has been failing subjects for the first time. On examination there is a coarse tremor of both outstretched arms that worsens on posture holding, mild dysarthria and clumsiness with rapid alternating movements. Viral hepatitis serology is negative, autoimmune liver serology is negative, ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal, and his serum caeruloplasmin is 0.19 g/L with a laboratory reference range of 0.20 to 0.60 g/L.

data_table.Examination: Coarse postural tremor of both arms, mild dysarthria, dysdiadochokinesis, no asterixis, no jaundice, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 118 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), bilirubin 16 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin 38 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.2), caeruloplasmin 0.19 g/L (0.20-0.60), ferritin 140 micrograms/L (30-300), hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody negative

lead_in: What combination of investigations is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Genetic sequencing of the responsible gene with parallel testing of both parents for carrier status
options.rationale: Molecular testing is valuable for family screening and for confirming ambiguous cases, but the large number of described mutations means results can take time and may be inconclusive. Biochemical confirmation is quicker in a symptomatic patient who needs treatment now. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Twenty four hour urinary copper excretion together with slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist
options.rationale: Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant and is normal or only marginally low in a substantial minority with this disorder, so a borderline value neither confirms nor excludes it and must never be used alone. Raised twenty four hour urinary copper excretion combined with corneal deposits seen on slit lamp examination, which are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement, establishes the diagnosis without liver biopsy in most cases. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Repeat serum caeruloplasmin with serum copper measurement after an interval of three months has passed
options.rationale: Repeating a test whose limitation is that it cannot exclude the disease adds nothing, and serum copper falls in parallel with caeruloplasmin so it carries the same weakness. The diagnostic value lies in urinary excretion and in the ocular examination. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with dedicated sequences through the basal ganglia structures
options.rationale: Brain imaging shows characteristic basal ganglia and midbrain changes and is important for assessing neurological involvement and for baseline comparison. It is supportive rather than diagnostic and does not establish disordered copper handling. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Liver biopsy with quantitative hepatic copper measurement as the initial confirmatory investigation here
options.rationale: Hepatic copper quantification is the reference standard and is used when non invasive testing is equivocal, but it carries procedural risk and is not the first step. Urinary copper with slit lamp examination resolves most cases without it. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport that presents between roughly five and forty years of age, with hepatic disease dominating in younger patients and neuropsychiatric features in older ones. The neurological presentation combines tremor, dysarthria, dystonia and clumsiness with personality change and deteriorating academic or work performance, and its combination with unexplained liver enzyme abnormality in a young adult is the pattern to recognise. The commonest diagnostic error is treating a normal or borderline caeruloplasmin as excluding the disease, since it is an acute phase reactant that rises with inflammation, oestrogen and pregnancy and is normal in a meaningful proportion of patients. Diagnosis therefore rests on raised twenty four hour urinary copper excretion together with slit lamp examination for corneal copper deposits, which are present in nearly all patients with neurological involvement, with hepatic copper quantification and genetic testing reserved for unresolved cases. Treatment is lifelong chelation or zinc, and first degree relatives must be screened because presymptomatic treatment prevents disease.
key_points: Liver disease plus a new movement disorder in a young adult should trigger the diagnosis
Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant and a normal value does not exclude the disease
Twenty four hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination is the practical diagnostic pair
Corneal deposits are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement
Screen first degree relatives, since presymptomatic treatment prevents disease
explanation.pearls: Suspect Wilson disease in any young patient with acute liver failure showing haemolysis with a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase and only modest transaminase elevation, because this pattern identifies fulminant presentations that will not survive without urgent transplant assessment and that are regularly misattributed to a viral or drug induced cause.

subtopic_detail: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy in an older woman
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 67 year old woman with eight months of watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels six to nine times a day including twice most nights. She has lost 4 kg and has occasional urgency with two episodes of incontinence.

There has never been blood in the stool. She has hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine and takes a proton pump inhibitor for reflux and a non steroidal anti inflammatory most days for knee pain. Coeliac serology with a normal immunoglobulin A level is negative, faecal calprotectin is 96 micrograms per gram, thyroid function is normal on treatment, and stool cultures including Clostridioides difficile toxin testing are negative. Colonoscopy performed today showed macroscopically normal mucosa throughout the colon and terminal ileum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non tender, no mass, normal perianal inspection and digital examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), faecal calprotectin 96 micrograms per gram (less than 50), tissue transglutaminase antibody negative with normal immunoglobulin A, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), stool cultures and Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, colonoscopy macroscopically normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen with pancreatic protocol to exclude a neuroendocrine tumour
options.rationale: Secretory diarrhoea from a hormone secreting tumour is rare and is usually accompanied by very high stool volumes, hypokalaemia and flushing. Pursuing it before completing the standard evaluation inverts the order of probability. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Start a gluten free diet empirically given that coeliac serology can be falsely negative in some patients
options.rationale: Serology performed with a normal immunoglobulin A level has good negative predictive value, and starting the diet before duodenal biopsy makes any later assessment for coeliac disease uninterpretable. An empirical dietary change is not a substitute for the histology that is now within reach. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease)

options.text: Take random biopsies from the right and left colon and send them for histological examination
options.rationale: Chronic non bloody watery diarrhoea with nocturnal symptoms and weight loss in an older woman with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy is the classic setting for microscopic colitis, which is invisible to the endoscopist and diagnosed only on histology. Biopsies must be taken from both the right and left colon because the changes are patchy and can be missed if sampling is limited to the rectosigmoid. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Commence a trial of loperamide titrated to stool frequency and review her symptoms in eight weeks time
options.rationale: Antimotility treatment is a reasonable adjunct once the diagnosis is known but here it would suppress symptoms in a patient whose diagnosis is undetermined after a full endoscopy. Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are features that call for a diagnosis rather than symptomatic control. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Arrange a selenium homocholic acid taurine scan to investigate bile acid diarrhoea as the underlying cause
options.rationale: Bile acid diarrhoea is a genuine and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery diarrhoea and this test is the standard way to demonstrate it. It is the right step only once mucosal disease has been excluded histologically, which requires the biopsies that have not yet been taken. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a leading cause of chronic watery diarrhoea in older adults, particularly women, and is defined by a macroscopically normal or near normal colonoscopy with characteristic histological changes of either a thickened subepithelial collagen band or a prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Because the endoscopic appearance is normal, the diagnosis is missed entirely unless random biopsies are taken, and sampling must include the right colon since disease can spare the rectosigmoid. Distinguishing features from functional diarrhoea are nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, urgency and incontinence, and a mildly raised faecal calprotectin is common. Recognised associations include coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease, and drugs including proton pump inhibitors, non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so a medication review is part of management. First line treatment is budesonide, alongside withdrawal of implicated drugs.
key_points: A normal colonoscopy does not exclude colitis; the diagnosis is histological
Biopsy both right and left colon because disease is patchy and can spare the rectosigmoid
Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss argue against a functional disorder
Proton pump inhibitors and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are recognised triggers
Budesonide is first line treatment alongside withdrawal of implicated drugs
explanation.pearls: Review the medication list before escalating treatment, because stopping a proton pump inhibitor or a regular non steroidal anti inflammatory can resolve the diarrhoea entirely in drug associated cases, and both are so commonly prescribed in this age group that their contribution is routinely overlooked.

subtopic_detail: New persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in a woman with established sicca symptoms
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 58 year old woman with a nine year history of dry eyes and dry mouth, positive anti-Ro antibodies and a previously positive labial gland biopsy. She has been stable on hydroxychloroquine and artificial tears.

She attends because her left parotid gland has been firm and enlarged for three months and has not fluctuated with meals. She has no fever, no toothache and no purulent discharge from the duct. Her complement C4 has fallen from 0.22 to 0.09 g/L over the past year and a serum protein electrophoresis performed six months ago showed a small immunoglobulin M kappa paraprotein. She has palpable non tender lymph nodes in the left cervical chain and reports drenching night sweats twice weekly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Firm non tender enlarged left parotid gland, two palpable left cervical lymph nodes each about 2 cm, no skin purpura, no splenomegaly, dry buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), lymphocytes 0.9 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0), lactate dehydrogenase 310 U/L (120-250), complement C4 0.09 g/L (0.15-0.55), serum protein electrophoresis showing a small immunoglobulin M kappa paraprotein, anti-Ro antibody positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for two weeks to treat bacterial infection of the parotid gland
options.rationale: Bacterial parotitis presents acutely with a tender hot gland and pus expressible from the duct, in a patient who is often febrile and dehydrated. Three months of painless firm enlargement without fever does not fit an infective process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange sialography with a course of gland massage and sialogogues for a presumed obstructing duct stone
options.rationale: A duct stone characteristically causes swelling and pain that worsen with eating and then settle, a pattern the history specifically excludes. Constant enlargement unrelated to meals argues against an obstructive cause. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Repeat the anti-Ro and anti-La antibody titres with a rheumatoid factor to reassess disease activity now
options.rationale: Autoantibody titres do not track disease activity in this condition and repeating them will not explain a parotid mass. Cryoglobulins and complement are the serological markers that carry prognostic weight, and the complement result is already abnormal. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange biopsy of the enlarged gland with imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
options.rationale: Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in this condition, with falling complement, a paraproteinaemia, lymphadenopathy and night sweats, is the described risk profile for transformation to lymphoma, which occurs in these patients at many times the background population rate. Tissue diagnosis with concurrent cross sectional staging is the step that determines treatment, and delay risks progression of a disease that is treatable when identified. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Increase the hydroxychloroquine dose and add pilocarpine to improve her glandular secretion and comfort
options.rationale: Secretagogues and hydroxychloroquine address sicca symptoms and fatigue but have no effect on a structural glandular mass. Intensifying symptomatic treatment while these particular features are present risks a long delay to a serious diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

explanation.summary: Sjogren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy causing dry eyes and dry mouth, most often in middle aged women, with anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and characteristic labial gland histology. Its most serious complication is transformation to non Hodgkin lymphoma, usually a mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma of the parotid, and the risk is many fold higher than in the general population. The recognised predictors are persistent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cryoglobulinaemia, a monoclonal paraprotein, low complement C4 and lymphopenia, and the falling complement here is among the strongest. A new persistent unilateral glandular mass in a patient with this diagnosis is therefore treated as lymphoma until histology proves otherwise, with biopsy and cross sectional staging arranged together. Recognising this risk at each review, rather than attributing every glandular change to the underlying autoimmune disease, is the practical clinical lesson.
key_points: Lymphoma risk in this condition is many times that of the general population
Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement is the single most important warning sign
Low complement C4, cryoglobulins, paraprotein and purpura are additional predictors
Autoantibody titres do not track disease activity and are not repeated for this purpose
Biopsy with concurrent cross sectional staging is the step that determines treatment
explanation.pearls: Measure complement C4 and cryoglobulins at review rather than repeating anti-Ro titres, because a falling C4 with cryoglobulinaemia identifies the subgroup at highest risk of lymphoma years before a mass appears and justifies closer surveillance of the glands and lymph nodes.

subtopic_detail: Persistent daytime sleepiness with sudden knee buckling during laughter
stem:
You are the respiratory and sleep registrar reviewing a 26 year old man referred with three years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness. He falls asleep in lectures and in the passenger seat and takes two naps most days, waking refreshed for an hour or two.

He describes his knees buckling and his jaw sagging for a few seconds whenever he laughs hard or is startled, remaining fully aware throughout. He also describes vivid frightening images as he falls asleep and occasional inability to move for a minute on waking. His body mass index is 23 kg per square metre, he has a Mallampati class 1 airway, and his partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing. His Epworth sleepiness score is 19. A polysomnogram performed last week showed an apnoea hypopnoea index of 2 per hour with normal oxygenation and reduced sleep latency.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 1, no tonsillar hypertrophy, no retrognathia, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Epworth sleepiness scale 19 out of 24, polysomnogram apnoea hypopnoea index 2 per hour with normal nocturnal oxygenation, ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat polysomnography with oesophageal pressure monitoring to detect upper airway resistance events
options.rationale: Upper airway resistance syndrome is worth considering in a sleepy patient with a normal apnoea hypopnoea index, but it does not explain cataplexy and this man has a favourable airway with no snoring. The overnight study has already answered the breathing question. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Electroencephalography with sleep deprivation to investigate the episodes as atonic epileptic seizures
options.rationale: Atonic seizures cause abrupt falls with impaired awareness and are not reliably provoked by emotion. Full preservation of awareness during a laughter triggered episode is the feature that separates cataplexy from a seizure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast to exclude a hypothalamic structural lesion present
options.rationale: Secondary narcolepsy from a hypothalamic lesion is rare and is suggested by additional endocrine or neurological deficits, which are absent on his normal examination. Imaging is added selectively rather than as the confirmatory test. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Actigraphy over two weeks with a sleep diary to assess for chronic insufficient sleep as the explanation
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness and actigraphy with a diary is the correct way to demonstrate it, and it is also required before latency testing to ensure the result is interpretable. It cannot account for cataplexy, which is close to specific for narcolepsy. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Multiple sleep latency testing performed on the day immediately following the overnight sleep study
options.rationale: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with preserved awareness is cataplexy, which alongside severe sleepiness, sleep onset hallucinations and sleep paralysis indicates narcolepsy, and the overnight study has already excluded significant sleep disordered breathing. Multiple sleep latency testing performed the day after an adequate overnight study confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating short mean sleep latency with rapid eye movement sleep onset periods. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy with cataplexy results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons and presents in adolescence or early adulthood with severe daytime sleepiness, refreshing short naps, hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis. Cataplexy is the near specific feature and is defined as sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most reliably laughter, with awareness fully preserved throughout, which distinguishes it from atonic seizures and from syncope. Diagnosis requires an adequate overnight polysomnogram, both to exclude another cause of sleepiness and to ensure sufficient sleep before testing, followed the next day by multiple sleep latency testing showing a short mean sleep latency and two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. A common pitfall is stopping at a normal apnoea hypopnoea index and telling the patient the sleep study was normal, when in fact the diagnosis requires the daytime study that follows. Management combines scheduled naps, treatment for sleepiness, agents for cataplexy, and explicit counselling on driving obligations.
key_points: Cataplexy is emotion triggered bilateral atonia with fully preserved awareness
Refreshing naps distinguish narcolepsy from most other causes of sleepiness
The overnight study excludes competing causes; the daytime latency study confirms
Two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods support the diagnosis
Preceding actigraphy is needed so insufficient sleep does not confound the result
explanation.pearls: Address driving explicitly at the diagnostic consultation, because Australian commercial and private licence standards require that excessive daytime sleepiness be reported and adequately treated, and documenting that advice protects both the patient and other road users while treatment is being established.
